title: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
subtitle: Among the first to believe, the first caliph, the second of two in the cave
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'the second of two'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3661 — the Prophet ﷺ tells the people to leave his companion Abu Bakr alone
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, including the cave
Sahih al-Bukhari 1400 — his caliphate and the wars of apostasy

chapters.heading: The One Who Never Hesitated
chapters.body: When the Prophet ﷺ first called, Abu Bakr believed, the seerah reports say, without hesitation — among the first to believe, and later the first of the ummah's leaders. The seerah reports say he bought and freed enslaved believers, among them Bilal, spending his wealth until his own house went without, and when the hijrah came, he was chosen: not for strength but for companionship. In the cave, Abu Bakr whispered: if they look down they will see us. And the Prophet ﷺ answered with the verse of the age: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). When others spoke harshly of Abu Bakr, the Prophet ﷺ told the people to leave his companion alone (Sahih al-Bukhari 3661).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Abu Bakr spent everything he had freeing people he didn't know. What would you empty your account for?

title: Umar ibn al-Khattab
subtitle: Al-Faruq — the one who separated truth from falsehood
sources: The Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise — Sahih al-Bukhari 3680
History (not a hadith): Umar's introduction of the Hijri calendar — Not yet scholar-reviewed
Sahih Muslim 2398 — 'if there were inspired ones in this ummah, Umar would be one of them'
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3686 — 'were there a prophet after me, it would be Umar' (hasan — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Strength Given to the Truth
chapters.body: He came to kill the Prophet ﷺ and left his brother — the conversion the tradition counts as the turning point of Makkah. Umar's Islam was force itself converted into force for Islam: the prayer moved into the open at the Kaaba the day he joined, and the Prophet's ﷺ dua for Islam to be strengthened through Umar (reported in the books of hadith) named the rest of his life. As caliph he walked the streets of Madinah at night with nothing but his cloak, checking on the needy, as the early histories relate (details not checked here) — amir al-mu'minin, commander of the believers, carrying the load the tradition captured in his own words: 'if a mule stumbles on the banks of the Euphrates, Umar will be asked about it on the Day of Judgment' (reported of Umar in the early histories; not from the six books). He fixed the calendar, built the garrison cities, opened the registers of the conquered lands as endowment for the ummah's poor, and was stabbed at dawn prayer by a slave. The Prophet ﷺ had said it of him in life: were there a prophet after me, it would be Umar (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3686 — hasan, Darussalam).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Umar carried responsibility for a mule on the Euphrates. What responsibility are you avoiding that is actually yours?

title: Uthman ibn Affan
subtitle: Dhun-Nurayn — the possessor of two lights, who equipped two armies and a standard
sources: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3701 — his gift for the army of hardship (hasan — Darussalam)
Qur'an 33:23 — 'among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah' (revealed at the pledge of ar-Ridwan)

chapters.heading: The Modest Millionaire
chapters.body: Uthman married two daughters of the Prophet ﷺ — Ruqayyah, then Umm Kulthum after her death — and earned the title Dhun-Nurayn, the Possessor of the Two Lights (early tradition; not from the six books). When the army of Tabuk lacked supplies, he donated a thousand dinars to equip it (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3701 — hasan, Darussalam). As caliph he completed what the previous two could not: the unification of the Qur'an into one master mushaf, the copies dispatched to every garrison city with the instruction that all variant readings be surrendered to it — the reason every Qur'an on earth today descends from a single archetype. He was besieged in his own house and killed there; the histories report that he forbade his household to fight and that he was reading the Qur'an (early histories; not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Uthman equipped an army in secret and asked no credit. When you give, do you need the receipt?

title: Ali ibn Abi Talib
subtitle: Among the first to believe — a young cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and the fourth caliph
sources: Sahih Muslim 2404 — 'you are to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me'

chapters.heading: The Boy Who Slept in the Prophet's Bed
chapters.body: On the night of the hijrah, with assassins at the door, Ali ibn Abi Talib lay in the Prophet's ﷺ bed (a seerah report), so the killers would strike the wrong man while the Prophet ﷺ slipped away; the reports say he returned the trusts left with the Prophet before leaving Makkah. He was among the first to embrace Islam as a boy, raised in the Prophet's ﷺ household — 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me' (Sahih Muslim 2404). At Badr he fought in the duels that opened the battle; at Khaybar he carried the banner the Prophet ﷺ gave 'to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger'; and his sermons were later collected for their eloquence (the attribution of the collections is disputed).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Ali slept in the Prophet's bed knowing swords were coming. What has your loyalty ever cost you?

title: Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib
subtitle: Sayyid al-Shuhada — the master of martyrs, the lion of Allah and His Messenger
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — his death at Uhud
Qur'an 16:126 — the verse that answered his mutilation

chapters.heading: The Uncle Who Became the Lion
chapters.body: When Abu Jahl insulted the Prophet ﷺ and a freedwoman told Hamza — hunting, still in his hunting dress — the uncle did not wait for deliberation. He walked to the Kaaba where Abu Jahl sat among his people, raised his bow, and struck him: will you insult him when I am upon his religion? — and the tradition records that some of Quraysh's own men wished, in that hour, that Hamza had kept silent long before. He embraced Islam the way he did everything: at full strength and without apology. At Badr he was the army's right wing; at Uhud he stood over the broken line until the spears found him. The Prophet ﷺ stood beside what the enemy had done to his uncle's body and wept, and said: I will mutilate seventy of them for you — until the revelation descended and forbade it forever (16:126). Hamza's title was fixed by that day: Sayyid al-Shuhada, the master of the martyrs.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Hamza used his strength the day he heard his nephew insulted. What strength of yours is waiting for the right cause?

title: Bilal ibn Rabah
subtitle: The caller of Islam — the muezzin whose footsteps were heard in Paradise
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the first muezzin of Islam

chapters.heading: Ahad, Under the Stone
chapters.body: He had been the slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, dragged onto the burning sand at noon with a boulder on his chest, and his answer was one word that has outlived every empire built on torture: Ahad — One. Abu Bakr passed by and purchased him — and freed him (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). At the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ had him climb the Kaaba to call the adhan (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). Bilal climbed the House of Allah — the house his former master had worshipped idols beside — and called the adhan over a city of new believers. He lived on in Madinah as the muezzin of the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, and after the Prophet's ﷺ death later reports tell of his grief and of a single adhan in Madinah (source not checked here). The Prophet ﷺ told him that he had heard the sound of his footsteps ahead of him in Paradise (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; numbers not re-checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Bilal's one word under a boulder became the adhan over the Kaaba. What is your one word that could outlive your circumstances?

title: Salman al-Farsi
subtitle: The seeker of a thousand miles — the trench was his idea
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the long search from Persia
Seerah sources: the counsel of the trench at the Battle of the Trench

chapters.heading: From Zoroastrian Fire-Worshipper to the Family of the House
chapters.body: Salman's road to Madinah took a lifetime: born to Zoroastrian fire-worshippers in Persia, he studied under a Christian bishop, was traded from master to master across Syria and Arabia, and carried at every stage one instruction from his teachers: a prophet is coming; his time is near; he will appear in the land of palm-trees between two lava-fields. When at last a caravan brought him to Yathrib — palms, two lava-tracts — he recognized the signs before he recognized the man: the seal of prophethood between the shoulders. The Prophet ﷺ heard his story of bondage and ransom and welcomed him as one of the household (reported in the seerah literature; not from the six books). At the Trench, when the alliance of ten thousand surrounded Madinah, it was Salman — the outsider, the Persian — whose counsel held the city: a trench along the open quarter, as the Persians build. The Muslims dug by night through the cold; Salman supervised; and the tradition records that the Prophet ﷺ worked beside him on the rock, striking three times — and each strike split a third of the rock — until light shone from the rock of Madinah. The idea that saved the city of the Prophet ﷺ came, the sources say, from a man of Persia.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Salman was a stranger with a foreign idea — and Madinah listened. What stranger's idea is your community dismissing right now?

title: Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah
subtitle: The trustee of this ummah — the man who pulled the Prophet's ﷺ own tooth at the Battle of Uhud
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari — 'every nation has a trustee, and the trustee of this ummah is Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah' (hadith number not re-checked in this build; Seerah report (source not checked) for the rest of the chapter)
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — his generalship in Syria

chapters.heading: The Pull of the Tooth
chapters.body: At Uhud, when the Prophet's ﷺ face was cut and a link of his helmet's chain was driven into his cheekbone, the companions crowded to pull it — and each, seeing his face, could not bear to be the one to hurt him. Abu Ubaidah gripped the link with his teeth and pulled, and his two front teeth fell out with it. That image — the companion sacrificing his own smile to spare the Prophet's ﷺ face — is the whole biography in one act. The Prophet ﷺ named him in a sentence that outranks armies: 'every nation has a trustee, and the trustee of this ummah is Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah' (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). In the wars of Syria, when the plague of Amwas struck his camp, he chose to stay with his army and die among them rather than survive by flight — and he died as he lived, in the line he had been trusted to hold.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Abu Ubaidah gave his own teeth to spare the Prophet's ﷺ pain. What small sacrifice of yours would mean more than a grand one?

title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
subtitle: The first to shoot an arrow in the path of Allah
sources: Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari — the Prophet's ﷺ words to Sa'd in battle (hadith number not re-checked in this build)
Qur'an 31:14-15 — revealed concerning his mother, 'if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge'
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Sa'd among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Arrow and the Mother
chapters.body: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas is remembered as the first to shoot an arrow in Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him in battle: shoot, Sa'd — may my father and mother be your ransom (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). His trial was not on the field but at home: his mother Hamna swore to fast in the heat, neither eating nor drinking, until he left Islam, and the revelation descended on his case: 'And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents; but if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them' (31:14-15). The Prophet ﷺ counted him among the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam). The histories report that he helped found Kufa, commanded at Qadisiyyah, and died near Madinah in old age (not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Sa'd's mother starved herself to pull him from Islam and the Qur'an answered his case. What do you do when the people you love most pull against your faith?

title: Talha and Zubayr
subtitle: The two who shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud with their own bodies
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — their stand at Uhud
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Talha and Zubayr among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)
Qur'an 3:154 — 'so that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts'

chapters.heading: The Living Shields
chapters.body: When the line broke at Uhud and the spears converged on the Prophet ﷺ, Talha ibn Ubaydullah and az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam threw themselves in front of him — Talha shielding him with his body (the reports say his hand was crippled that day) The Prophet ﷺ said of Talha that day: whoever wishes to see a man walking on the ground who has completed his reward, let him look at Talha (reported in the hadith literature; the number was not verified). Zubayr was the first to draw a sword for Islam — at the very first confrontation in Makkah, the tradition says, he unsheathed first — and married Asma, the daughter of Abu Bakr (see her story). Talha was among the richest of the companions and, the reports say, among the most generous (seerah; details not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Talha's hand hung useless from shielding the Prophet ﷺ. What are you willing to take a hit for?

title: Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf
subtitle: The merchant of the ummah — who gave his garden as dowry and fed armies
sources: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the caravan that came at Madinah's famine
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3749 — the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf (hasan — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Commerce as Worship
chapters.body: When the Ansar offered to split their wealth with the Muhajirun, Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf answered: show me the market — and the tradition records that by the week's end he had earned and married, with a dowry of gold from his own trade, and Sa'd ibn Rabi' offered him half of everything. His genius was not merely earning: it was knowing whom earnings belonged to. The reports tell of a caravan of his arriving from Syria and being given away in charity (a seerah report; the size of the caravan and the wording were not checked here). The Prophet ﷺ named him among the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam), and prayed for him (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3749 — hasan, Darussalam). Reports say he left large bequests for charity (not checked here) — wealth as a river, not a reservoir.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Abdur-Rahman knew every poor family in Madinah by name. Do you know the names of the struggling people on your own street?

title: Sa'id ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Harithah
subtitle: The tenth of the ten — and the beloved freedman whom Allah named
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — Zayd, the first freedman in Islam, 'adopted' then returned to his name by revelation
Qur'an 33:4-5 — 'call them by their fathers' (revealed for Zayd)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Sa'id ibn Zayd among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Two Names, Two Honors
chapters.body: Zayd ibn Harithah was kidnapped as a child and sold in Makkah, given to Khadijah, and given by her to the Prophet ﷺ — who freed him and kept him as a son until, years later, Zayd's actual father and uncles arrived in Makkah to ransom him home. Zayd chose: I will not leave this man for any people on earth — and the Prophet ﷺ took him to the Kaaba and announced before Quraysh: bear witness, this is my son, inheriting from me (Ibn Ishaq). When revelation later abolished adoption, Zayd's name itself became the test case: 'Call them by their fathers — that is more just in the sight of Allah' (33:5), and Zayd ibn Muhammad became Zayd ibn Harithah — the only companion named in the Qur'an (33:37). He was the first of the three commanders killed at Mu'tah, and the Prophet ﷺ wept for him (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here). Sa'id ibn Zayd, the tenth of the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam), embraced Islam early; the seerah reports say it was in his house, with his wife Fatima bint al-Khattab, Umar's sister, that Umar heard the recitation that led to his conversion.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Zayd chose the Prophet ﷺ over his own father, then carried his father's name forever. What does that teach about love that costs nothing of honor?

title: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud
subtitle: The shepherd of Uqbah — a teacher of the Qur'an
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3808 — the Prophet ﷺ names four companions to learn the Qur'an from, among them Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b

chapters.heading: The Boy Who Learned From the Prophet ﷺ
chapters.body: He was a thin shepherd boy of Makkah when the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr passed him at Uqbah, and Muhammad ﷺ asked him for milk the boy did not own — and the ewe that had no milk flowed, and the boy watched prophecy work before he ever heard a verse. Ibn Mas'ud attached himself to the Prophet's ﷺ household as a servant and a shadow, running errands and absorbing revelation until he memorized directly from the Messenger himself; the tradition counts him among the four from whom the ummah was told to learn the Qur'an, among them Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy (Sahih al-Bukhari 3808). When Makkah demanded: who will recite for us? — the companions knew the price of volunteering, and Ibn Mas'ud volunteered, though he had no clan to protect him (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). He recited Surah Ar-Rahman at the Kaaba until Quraysh beat him into unconsciousness. Many rulings of prayer and purification are transmitted through his narrations.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Ibn Mas'ud volunteered knowing the beating was certain. When did you last volunteer first for something costly?

title: Ammar ibn Yasir
subtitle: The son of Sumayyah — driven from paradise to paradise
sources: Qur'an 16:106 — 'except for one who is forced, while his heart is secure in faith' (revealed for Ammar)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3798 — the Prophet's ﷺ welcome of Ammar (hasan — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Forced Words, Secure Heart
chapters.body: His mother Sumayyah was the first martyr of Islam; his father Yasir was killed beside her; and Ammar was stretched on the burning sand of Makkah until the words of unbelief were forced from his tongue while his heart held fast. The commentators report that 16:106 was revealed about him ('except for one who is forced while his heart is secure in faith'), and the seerah reports tell that the Prophet ﷺ comforted him. At the Trench he worked until his own people could not recognize him under the dust, and the Prophet ﷺ welcomed him as the pure and purified (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3798 — hasan, Darussalam). Years later Ammar was killed at Siffin, fighting alongside Ali; a hadith that a rebelling party would kill him is reported (Sahih Muslim; number not re-checked here) and is remembered in connection with his death. How it applies is a matter scholars have discussed. The son of the first martyr became its most foretold one.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Ammar's worst moment became a verse of mercy. What could your worst moment become?

title: Abu Hurayrah
subtitle: The keeper of the Prophet's ﷺ words — more narrations than any companion
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari — he is among its most frequent narrators (hadith number not re-checked in this build)
Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — Abu Hurayrah's own account of why he narrated so much (hadith numbers not re-checked in this build)

chapters.heading: Hunger and Memory
chapters.body: He arrived in Madinah with nothing — no clan, no property, no trade — and accepted hunger as the price of companionship: 'I would be overtaken by hunger and would fall on my belly on the road, and the people would say: the devil has possessed him — but it was only hunger' (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). He ate with the people of Suffa, prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ in every prayer he could reach, and trained himself as a living archive, later explaining his unmatched memory: when the emigrants of Makkah were busy with trade and the Ansar with their orchards, I was free and hungry — I was present where they were absent (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The scholars count more than five thousand narrations from him — more than any companion, male or female. His kunya, Abu Hurayrah, 'father of the kitten', is said to come from a kitten he kept (a report whose source was not checked here). The man who memorized the most was the man who needed the most.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Abu Hurayrah's poverty became the ummah's library. What is your limitation that could become your offering?

title: Anas ibn Malik
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ attendant for ten years — 'he was kind to me'
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners — Anas: 'he never once said to me even "uff"' (hadith number not re-checked in this build)
Sahih al-Bukhari — Anas's account of serving the Prophet ﷺ (hadith number not re-checked in this build)

chapters.heading: Ten Years Without 'Uff'
chapters.body: His mother Umm Sulaym brought him to the Prophet ﷺ as a boy of ten and said: O Messenger of Allah, Anas is a smart boy; let him serve you. He entered the household as an errand-boy and left it as one of the greatest narrators of the age — and his entire testimony of those ten years compresses into a sentence that has defined Islamic manners ever since: 'He never once said to me, even about a thing I had broken or a thing I had failed to do: even so much as 'uff.' And he never said about anything: why did you do it? — nor about a thing I had not done: why did you not do it?' (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners). Serving the best of creation, Anas said, was better than serving any king, for by Allah, he never hit me, never struck me, never insulted me (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). The boy who tied the Prophet's ﷺ sandals grew into the man whose narrations carry the sunnah of the household into every book of law — and his mother's wager, offering her son's service to the Messenger, became one of the most honored investments in the ummah's history.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Ten years of service without one harsh word. What would change in your home if 'uff' disappeared for ten days?

title: Abdullah ibn Abbas
subtitle: Habr al-ummah — the scholar of the ummah, the interpreter of the Qur'an
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 75 — the Prophet's ﷺ embrace of Ibn Abbas and dua for his knowledge of the Qur'an
Sahih al-Bukhari 143 — the Prophet's ﷺ dua for his understanding of the religion

chapters.heading: The Cousin Allah Taught
chapters.body: He was thirteen when the Prophet ﷺ died, a boy who had crept close to every gathering — and Muhammad ﷺ, seeing him near, would call him close and make dua over him — for understanding of the religion (Sahih al-Bukhari 143) and for knowledge of the Qur'an (Sahih al-Bukhari 75). The dua outlived the boy's youth and outgrew every expectation: within a generation, Ibn Abbas became the standard of tafsir, the man before whom the senior companions sat as students — Umar appointed him to the council of Madinah's jurists while he was still in his twenties, and the caliph said the people learn from him though he is young (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). The tradition remembers him as the model of tafsir, and many early commentaries trace their explanations back to him (the chains vary in strength; not checked here). The Prophet's ﷺ house gave the ummah a dynasty of scholarship from a teenage cousin: the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for a boy became a library for the ummah.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ prayed for a boy's understanding and a library was born. Whose potential could your dua unlock?

title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
subtitle: The scholar of Yemen — 'you are going to a people of the Book'
sources: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1327 — the order of the judge: the Book, the sunnah, then one's own reasoning (daʿif — Darussalam)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — the Prophet's ﷺ praise of Mu'adh's knowledge of the lawful and unlawful (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Judge Who Took Revelation With Him
chapters.body: He was the young Ansari the Prophet ﷺ sent alone to govern and judge the whole of Yemen, and at the parting the Prophet ﷺ walked beside his saddle for miles, teaching him the methodology that judges a million questions: by the Book of Allah — and if not found? — by the sunnah — and if not found? — then strive with your judgment, and do not shy from it, for the Prophet said: praise be to Allah who has enabled the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to please the Messenger of Allah (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1327 — daʿif, Darussalam; the report is widely discussed). The scholars count Mu'adh the most learned of the ummah in halal and haram (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — sahih, Darussalam); he died young, in the plague of Amwas. The student of the farewell became the teacher of the schools.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Mu'adh was told: judge by the Book, then the sunnah, then your honest striving. What decision are you avoiding that honest striving would settle?

title: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
subtitle: The keeper of the secrets — the man who knew the hypocrites by name
sources: Sahih Muslim — Hudhayfah sent to scout the enemy camp on the night of the Trench (hadith number not re-checked in this build)
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the pledge of the secrets at the Trench

chapters.heading: Entrusted With the Names
chapters.body: His father al-Yaman was killed by mistake by Muslims at Uhud, and Hudhayfah forgave them (a report in Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here). The Prophet ﷺ took him as a confidant: on the freezing night of the Trench he sent Hudhayfah to learn what the enemy was doing (reported in Sahih Muslim). Of all the companions, only Hudhayfah was entrusted with the roster of the hypocrites according to the reports (a report in Sahih Muslim speaks of his knowledge of them; number not checked here). Umar is reported to have asked whether he himself was among them. He died around the year 36 of the Hijrah (histories; date not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Hudhayfah carried a list that could have made him powerful, and died with it secret. What would you do with a secret that powerful?

title: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
subtitle: The branded one — iron pressed on his back while the Prophet ﷺ sat beside him
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3612 — his complaint and the Prophet's ﷺ answer
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the branding by the slave-masters of Makkah

chapters.heading: The Iron and the Answer
chapters.body: He was a blacksmith's slave, and his masters of Makkah invented for him what they invented for no other: they dragged the iron of his own forge out of his fire and pressed it onto his bare back until it cooled, and they did it again, and again. In Bukhari 3612 Khabbab says that they complained to the Prophet ﷺ of what they were suffering from the polytheists while he was resting in the shade of the Kaaba, and asked: will you not ask Allah for help for us? He ﷺ sat up and answered with the prophecy that holds every wounded generation upright: 'among those before you, a man would be seized and a saw of iron laid upon the crown of his head and he would be sawn in two, and that would not turn him from his religion. By Allah, this religion will be completed until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt fearing nothing but Allah — and the wolf for his sheep' (Bukhari 3612). Khabbab outlived the Prophet ﷺ and, the histories say, lived to see Islam spread widely (not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ promised relief in a generation, not a moment. What long game are you quitting too early?

title: Suhayb ar-Rumi
subtitle: The Byzantine who bought his own life from Quraysh — and laughed last
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the bargain at the gate of Makkah

chapters.heading: Everything I Own for Myself
chapters.body: He was born to Byzantine parents, captured as a boy, sold in Arabia, and won his own freedom by craft — an archer, a merchant, and a polyglot who had lived inside three civilizations before he ever heard the Qur'an. When he embraced Islam, Quraysh blocked his emigration as they blocked the rest, and as he stood at the gate of Makkah with everything he owned loaded, they said: you came to us a penniless boy and grew rich among us — you go with your religion only if you leave your wealth. Suhayb emptied his caravan into their hands and walked north, and the early sources relate that the Prophet ﷺ, hearing it, said the trade was profitable (seerah report; not from the six books). At Badr he fought; at Uhud he fought; and the reports say that when Umar was stabbed he appointed Suhayb to lead the prayers until the council chose a successor (history; not checked here). The boy Byzantium lost, Arabia enslaved, and Makkah robbed led the prayers in a dark hour, and died in Madinah in the later years of the Rashidun, according to the histories.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Suhayb traded everything visible for everything real. What 'everything' are you holding that you know is worth less than what it costs?

title: Mus'ab ibn Umair
subtitle: The flower of Quraysh who gave up silk for a woolen cloak
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — his mission to Madinah and the death at Uhud
Sahih al-Bukhari — Mus'ab buried in a single cloak after Uhud (hadith number not re-checked in this build)

chapters.heading: From the Perfumed Youth to the First Ambassador
chapters.body: He was the most pampered youth of Makkah — his mother combed the city for the finest cloth, and he went out trailing perfume and silk, the envy of every merchant's son. Islam took him, and his mother took his wardrobe: she locked him out of the house until he chose between her and the Prophet ﷺ — and he chose, and the silk was gone. After the first pledge of Aqabah, Mus'ab was sent to Yathrib as Islam's first ambassador — a boy sent to teach a city — and the seerah records that he taught, led the prayer, and carried the invitation until the day Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's entire clan embraced Islam in a single morning. At Uhud he carried the banner of the Muslims, and when the mêlée took him, he lay under the fallen with his hand severed, reciting: Muhammad is only a Messenger; messengers have passed on before him — until the verse was complete in him and he was (3:144; Ibn Ishaq). The Prophet ﷺ ordered him buried where he fell, one cloth for a shroud — and the man who had once worn two robes of silk was wound in a single garment, and the Prophet ﷺ stood over his grave and said: I saw you in Makkah, with no one more pampered in clothing and perfume than you — and I see you today, the shroud barely covering you (the burial in a single cloth is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari; the words are reported in the seerah literature).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Mus'ab traded silk for a shroud and called it profit. What pampering could you trade for a cause?

title: Abdullah ibn Umar
subtitle: The pilgrim of the ummah — a careful follower of the sunnah
sources: No hadith citation: biographical summary — Not yet scholar-reviewed

chapters.heading: The Man Who Heard and Held
chapters.body: He was the son of the caliph and could have been a king; instead he became the most careful listener the ummah ever produced. The sources remember him as a careful follower of what he heard from the Prophet ﷺ (this chapter is a reflection; the particular anecdotes it once told had no source and are not repeated). The son of the strongest man became the gentlest of the strict.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: One heard prohibition held for a lifetime, at the cost of profit. What principle do you bend the moment it costs you?

title: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
subtitle: The master reciter — named by the Prophet ﷺ among those to learn the Qur'an from
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — 'Allah has commanded me to recite to you' (hadith numbers not re-checked in this build)

chapters.heading: The Man Who Learned Directly
chapters.body: He was a scribe of revelation and one of the four arch-reciters, and the tradition preserves the night that made him: the Prophet ﷺ woke him and said: Allah has commanded me to recite to you — and Ubayy wept: was I named to you, O Messenger of Allah? — and the Prophet ﷺ said: yes, you were named to me (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Many recitation chains are traced back to him (not checked here).
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Ubayy knew himself better than his flatterers did. When did you last audit yourself against your own praise?

title: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari
subtitle: The lone voice — 'the earth is vast'
sources: Sahih Muslim 55 — 'the religion is sincerity' (narrated by Tamim al-Dari)

chapters.heading: The Ascetic Who Learned the Middle
chapters.body: He came out of the desert of Ghifar with a brother and a question — tell me of this new word — and embraced Islam on the strength of one hearing, then rode back to his tribe alone, a believer in a nation of robbers, and argued his own people into the faith one fireside at a time. His piety was absolute and his tongue was absolute, and the two together made him the conscience that would not be seated: he spoke against the accumulation of wealth in the caliphate of Uthman until the cities rang, and the histories report that he went to al-Rabadhah, where he lived the rest of his life (Sahih al-Bukhari has a related account; number not re-checked here). The Muslims of the city took turns riding out to him with food and news. The Prophet ﷺ taught the ummah that the religion is sincerity — to Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common people (Sahih Muslim 55, narrated by Tamim al-Dari).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Abu Dharr chose exile over silence. When is speaking up worth losing everything — and when is the middle the braver place?

title: The Third in the Cave
subtitle: Two men hid in a cave while the hunters stood at the entrance — and Allah was the third
sources: Qur'an 9:40
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653

chapters.heading: The Hunt at the Threshold
chapters.body: On the night of the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr while the bounty-hunters stood so close that Abu Bakr whispered that if one of them looked down he would see them. 'O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?' the Prophet answered (Bukhari 3653) — the Qur'an preserves the same calm: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). The most documented hiding place in history, and the hunted man spent his fear on his companion's comfort.

chapters.heading: The Web Added by Later Tradition
chapters.body: Later tradition adds that a spider had woven its web at the entrance and a dove had nested there; this is not in the Qur'an or in Sahih al-Bukhari 3653 and no chain was verified for this audit. Whatever one holds of that detail, the Qur'an's verdict stands untouched: 'If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two — when they were in the cave, he said to his companion: do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). The aid arrived before the help did.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

chapters.heading: What the Cave Decided
chapters.body: A spider's thread is not a strategy. Two men and a God are not an army. Yet Madinah was built from that cave, and from Madinah the world changed. The lesson the cave teaches is not that danger is unreal — it is that companionship with Allah reframes the arithmetic of odds. Abu Bakr's rank of as-Siddiq was sealed before any battle was won: he believed in the cave, at the hour when belief was only a voice in the dark.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Where is our 'cave' right now — and who is our third?
